papers.title: Green Tastes, Beliefs, and Portfolios: Evidence from Synthetic Investors
papers.abstract: We use LLMs as synthetic survey respondents to elicit green tastes, return beliefs, portfolio allocations, and investment motives from 480 retail and 60 institutional investor identities. Compared with retail, institutions report weaker tastes yet greener portfolio tilts, citing outside pressure. A greener tilt therefore need not indicate a stronger taste for greenness. Retail tastes depend mostly on political affiliation, institutional tastes on type and geography. Beliefs differ across the three ESG dimensions, with high-governance portfolios expected to outperform. We reconstruct survey responses under 2014--2025 information environments using date-masked information modules shuffled across years. Tastes vary little over time, but beliefs about green portfolios become more pessimistic after 2020. The two reconstructed series relate to different real-world data: tastes to measures of green demand, beliefs to measures of attention.

papers.title: Pollution Monitoring and the Pricing of Environmental Risk in Firms
papers.abstract: Pricing firms’ environmental risk is central to ensuring that capital is efficiently allocated. We examine whether an increase in the salience of pollution information affects the beliefs and perceived valuations of financially sophisticated agents—financial analysts—regarding the environmental risks faced by the firms they cover. Exploiting the staggered rollout of China's ambient air quality monitoring program, we show that when monitoring is introduced in a city, analysts based there become substantially more likely to discuss air pollution. These changes in attention are reflected in stock prices: reports issued by treated analysts generate more negative market reactions for brown firms and more positive reactions for green firms, with little change for environmentally neutral firms. These price responses do not subsequently reverse. Treated analysts increase their information acquisition through corporate site visits and issue less favorable assessments of brown firms and more favorable assessments of green firms. Our findings show that ambient environmental monitoring can affect asset prices by making environmental risks more salient and inducing greater information production about their implications for firm value.

papers.title: Coase Meets Negishi: Property Rights, Welfare Weights, and Distributional Consequences in Climate Economics
papers.abstract: We develop a property-rights based approach for defining welfare weights in economic models of climate change. Whether there is a "right to pollute" or a "right to no pollution" is increasingly contested in legislatures, courts, and international climate negotiations. We show how these notions of property rights can provide the basis for "Coasean welfare weights" that are applicable in multilateral public goods settings. Distributional questions are addressed through positive analysis, conditional on property rights, rather than normative views about redistribution. The implied transfers are consistent with a bargained solution over the net benefits of addressing climate change and reflect the value of property rights over emissions. The approach defines efficient allocations that generate Pareto improvements, in contrast to commonly used Negishi weights. We implement the approach in a global integrated assessment model to quantify what countries have at stake in ongoing political and legal debates about emissions-related property rights.
